script: Try to tickle yourself. Right now. Go on. Nothing, right? There's a reason. In the late nineteen nineties, neuroscientist Sarah-Jayne Blakemore and her team built a tickle robot. People moved a handle, and the robot stroked their palm with soft foam. When it copied their movement instantly, it barely tickled. Then they added a tiny delay. A fifth of a second. Suddenly, it tickled more. Your brain predicts every move you make. When it sees a touch coming, it turns the feeling down. Your own hand can't surprise you. And a tickle without surprise is just a touch. Bet you're about to try it again.
